name: Texas sharpshooter fallacy
aliases: Painting the target around the bullet hole
statement: The Texas sharpshooter fallacy is drawing the target after the shots have landed, then reporting the pattern as though it had been predicted in advance.
meaning: This is a fault in the order of operations rather than in a mind. A hypothesis chosen after the data are seen has already used up the evidence that would test it, so the p value attached to it no longer means what it says. The barn wall is the space of comparisons that could have been made: subgroups, outcome measures, exclusion rules, the boundaries of a map, the window of years. Fixing those before looking makes one shot count. Choosing them after looking makes the hit certain and uninformative. Research methodology calls the same move HARKing, hypothesising after the results are known, a term Norbert Kerr coined in 1998 for presenting a post hoc hypothesis as if it had been a priori. Most of the evidence here is about how research is done. One economics experiment, described below, tests people directly. The clustering illusion, entry 60, covers perceiving groupings in random data, and apophenia, entry 41, has its own page. The garden of forking paths, entry 560, covers the narrower claim that a single honest analysis is enough to break a p value. The sharpshooter is the further step of building a claim on the grouping and presenting it as a prediction.

origin.note: Grufferman's paper on clustering in Hodgkin's disease carries the story in the scientific literature. It compares a posteriori clusters to 'the story of the Texas sharpshooter who would shoot his rifle at the side of a barn and then carefully draw a target around each bullet-hole'. The paper was not obtained for this entry. Author, journal, volume 39 issue S4 and pages 1829-1833 were confirmed at Crossref, and the wording is quoted from Barry Popik's etymological page, which reproduces it from a Decision Science News post of 29 August 2012. Neither Popik nor that post claims it is the earliest use, and Popik's own summary says only that the story has been cited in print since at least 1977. Popik dates 'Texas sharpshooter effect' to Schottenfeld and Fraumeni's Cancer Epidemiology and Prevention in 1982, page 744, and 'Texas sharpshooter fallacy' to Elwood and colleagues in 1992, page 248, who credit the image to Grufferman in 1982. The story is older than the Texan. John Venn gives it without a name in chapter XIV of The Logic of Chance, on fallacies. Kenneth Rothman's 1990 address to a conference on disease clusters is the source Goodman and colleagues take the metaphor from.

evidence: Cancer clusters are the case with the most counting behind it. Goodman and colleagues reviewed 428 publicly available US cluster investigations from January 1990 to September 2011, covering 567 cancers of concern. An increase in incidence was confirmed for 72 of them, 13%. Three were linked to a hypothesised exposure with variable degrees of certainty, and one investigation revealed a clear cause. Their conclusion is that extensive efforts to find causes of community cancer clusters have not been successful. They put the structural fault in words quoted from the editorial to the 1989 national conference proceedings. That editorial called a cluster investigation reactive, working often from 'data toward a hypothesis, in stark contrast to the scientific method of developing a hypothesis first and then gathering data to confirm or deny it'. It is alongside that passage that they invoke Rothman's sharpshooter, 'who first fires his bullet and only then draws the target'. Two figures in their paper are quoted from others and are repeated at that remove here. From Thun and Sinks they take an estimate of upwards of 1,000 to 2,000 inquiries about perceived disease clusters in a given year, most of them about cancer. From Williams they take a Minnesota analysis of cancer incidence by county that identified 100,000 clusters for 85 cancers, of which 10,000 exceeded the statewide rate at least twofold and 1,500 were statistically significant. The arithmetic underneath is the multiple comparisons problem. Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn ran 15,000 simulations for each of four ordinary analytic choices, on a baseline two-condition design with 20 observations per cell. At p < .05, flexibility between two dependent variables correlated at r = .50 gives 9.5%. Adding ten observations per cell and testing again gives 7.7%. Controlling or not controlling for gender gives 11.7%, and dropping one of three conditions gives 12.6%. All four together give 60.7%. The same paper reports two real experiments on University of Pennsylvania undergraduates. Thirty heard either a children's song or a control track, and those given the children's song felt older, F(1, 27) = 5.06, p = .033. In the second, 20 participants who heard 'When I'm Sixty-Four' came out nearly a year and a half younger by their stated birth dates than those given the control. The adjusted means were 20.1 against 21.5 years, F(1, 17) = 4.92, p = .040. The paper then discloses its own workings in a table. Thirty-four undergraduates were run across three conditions and 20 across two were reported. The survey carried eleven measures rather than two, and analyses were run after every session of about ten participants. Without father's age as a covariate the age result disappears, F(1, 18) = 1.01, p = .33. On how often the target moves in practice, John, Loewenstein and Prelec e-mailed 5,964 American academic psychologists and got 2,155 respondents, a response rate of 36%. Asked whether they had reported an unexpected finding as having been predicted from the start, 27.0% said yes in the control group and 35.0% under an incentive scheme for truthful answers, an odds ratio of 1.45. The one experiment found here that puts the question to people is Mitesh Kataria's. Two hundred and forty-three students recruited through ORSEE in Jena in May 2013 were split evenly across three treatments of 81. All read the same scenario about a model of El Nino events with the same overall hit rate. Those told the model had only been fitted to old data judged it 65% likely to be right in future. Those told five of its hits came from predictions made after it was built judged it 77% likely. The difference is significant on a two-sided Mann-Whitney test at p = 0.030. Shown both side by side, subjects raised the fitted model to 72% and left the predicting model at 76%, so the gap narrows when the comparison is explicit. Sixty percent of subjects said the predicting scientist was no more knowledgeable, and among those the gap between the two models was not significant. Kataria reads the result as a departure from Bayesian confirmation theory, in which accommodated and predicted evidence confirm equally. Thompson takes the same fallacy into forensic DNA. His abstract argues from casework, informal and naturalistic experiments and analysts' own testimony that the criteria for a match get shifted once a suspect's profile is known, which makes matches look more probative than they are. The crowdsourced-analysis evidence that this entry used to carry sits at entry 560.

replication.headline: One experiment tests people directly and no attempt to repeat it was found. Kataria's 243 students rated a model fitted to old data 65% likely to be right in future against 77% for one that predicted new data.
replication.detail: Kataria's experiment has not been repeated. OpenCitations lists two works citing the published 2016 version, a games-adaptation paper and a preregistration template, and neither re-runs the design. Three things stand in place of a replication record. The first is the crowdsourced-analysis literature, which repeats a demonstration rather than an effect and is set out at entry 560. The second and third are before-and-after comparisons from fields that changed the order of hypothesis and data. Kaplan and Irvin identified 55 large NHLBI trials of drugs or dietary supplements for cardiovascular disease between 1970 and 2012. Of the 30 published before 2000, 17 (57%) reported a benefit on the primary outcome; of the 25 published after, 2 (8%) did, with a chi-square of 12.2 on 1 degree of freedom, p = 0.0005. Their two groups are defined by registration as well as by date, the earlier 30 unregistered and the later 25 preregistered at clinicaltrials.gov, and 7 of the 30 earlier publications did not identify a primary outcome at all. Scheel, Schijen and Lakens compared the 71 published Registered Reports in psychology available as of November 2018 with a random sample of 152 hypothesis-testing studies from the standard literature. Taking the first hypothesis of each article, 146 of 152 standard reports were positive, 96.05%, against 31 of 71 Registered Reports, 43.66%. Neither comparison is randomised, and both mix the effect of fixing the target with the effect of removing publication bias.

limits: One experiment on volunteers is a thin base, it was run on students in a single German city, and its published version could not be obtained, so the figures here come from the 2013 Jena working paper. Kataria's finding also points away from the fallacy as usually told: his subjects discounted a model fitted after the fact rather than being fooled by it. The search for further experiments on individual susceptibility ran on 17 August 2026 across Europe PMC, PubMed, Crossref, the OSF preprint index and general web search. It paired the fallacy and HARKing with terms for experiments, vignettes, susceptibility and post hoc hypothesising. Europe PMC returns 37 records for the phrase 'Texas sharpshooter' and PubMed 22, and pairing the phrase with experiment or participants in title or abstract at PubMed returns none. The OSF preprint index returns three records for HARKing and none for the sharpshooter. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar refused requests during this check and were not searched. Adjacent work exists on hindsight bias, on perceived randomness and on questionable research practices, and none of it found here uses this fallacy as its outcome measure. Four documents were not obtained: Grufferman's 1977 paper, quoted here from Popik quoting Decision Science News; Rothman's 1990 conference address, quoted here through Goodman and colleagues; Evers's 2017 editorial, which has no abstract at Europe PMC and whose publisher PDF returned 403; and Thompson's full text, of which only the abstract was read, twice, at the publisher. Simmons was read from a mirrored PDF rather than the SAGE version. Venn's barn-door passage was read in the Project Gutenberg transcription of the third edition of 1888. Wagenmakers places it at page 259 of the 1866 first edition, which was not checked. The cluster figures describe what investigations concluded, not the true rate of environmental causes, and a study that fails to find a cause has not shown there was none. The two before-and-after comparisons are observational, and the trial result is confined to one funder and one disease area.
misreadings: The commonest error is to treat any post hoc analysis as the fallacy. Exploring data is how hypotheses are found, and Gelman and Loken say plainly that it is good scientific practice to refine one's research hypotheses in light of the data. The fallacy is the claim of confirmatory strength for a target drawn afterwards, which is a claim about what the number means rather than about how it was obtained. A second error runs the other way, reading the fallacy as an accusation of cheating. Gelman and Loken's argument is that a researcher who performs one honest analysis, with no fishing and no intent, produces an invalid p value whenever a different data set would have led to a different analysis. Their own recommendation where preregistration is impractical is to analyse all the relevant comparisons rather than one. That the costs are large is itself disputed. Mark Rubin reviews Kerr's twelve potential costs of HARKing and argues they are misconceived, misattributed, lacking evidence, or already met by peer review and open materials, concluding that it is premature to assume HARKing has caused low replication rates. The name is also taken more literally than it deserves. Popik's trace turns up no actual marksman, and Wagenmakers places the story in Venn in 1866 with no Texas in it. Wagenmakers cites Cicero as well and then separates the two cases: Cicero's archer draws the target first and shoots many arrows, which is the multiple comparisons problem, while the sharpshooter needs one shot. Cancer clusters attract the last confusion. The finding that few investigations identify a cause is a statement about what the method can resolve, given small numbers and boundaries drawn after the cases are known. It is not a verdict on any particular community's suspicion.

sources.text: Grufferman, S. (1977). Clustering and aggregation of exposures in Hodgkin's disease. Cancer, 39(S4), 1829-1833. Not obtained; the Wiley PDF returned 403. Cited for the sharpshooter story in the scientific literature, with the wording taken from Popik. Author, journal, volume, issue and pages confirmed at Crossref.

Popik, B. (2013). Texas Sharpshooter Fallacy. The Big Apple, 9 March. Etymological trace giving the 1977 Grufferman quotation, which it reproduces from a Decision Science News post of 29 August 2012, plus 'Texas sharpshooter effect' in 1982, 'Texas sharpshooter fallacy' in 1992 and 'Texas sharpshooter problem' in 1995.
Venn, J. (1888). The Logic of Chance, 3rd edition. Chapter XIV, Fallacies. The barn-door passage was read in the Project Gutenberg transcription of this edition.

Wagenmakers, E.-J. (2018). Origin of the Texas Sharpshooter. Bayesian Spectacles, 11 January. Traces the metaphor to Venn's first edition of 1866, page 259, and distinguishes it from a passage in Cicero's De divinatione.

Rothman, K. J. (1990). A sobering start for the cluster busters' conference. American Journal of Epidemiology, 132(supp1), 6-13. No abstract; not obtained, and no open copy was listed at Unpaywall. Quoted here through Goodman et al. (2012).

Goodman, M., Naiman, J. S., Goodman, D., & LaKind, J. S. (2012). Cancer clusters in the USA: What do the last twenty years of state and federal investigations tell us? Critical Reviews in Toxicology, 42(6), 474-490. Read as the PubMed Central full text, PMC3408895. The inquiry estimate and the Minnesota counts are quoted inside it from Thun and Sinks and from Williams respectively, and are used here at that remove.

Simmons, J. P., Nelson, L. D., & Simonsohn, U. (2011). False-Positive Psychology: Undisclosed Flexibility in Data Collection and Analysis Allows Presenting Anything as Significant. Psychological Science, 22(11), 1359-1366. Table 1, Table 3 and both experiments read from a mirrored PDF of the typeset article; the SAGE copy returned 403.

John, L. K., Loewenstein, G., & Prelec, D. (2012). Measuring the Prevalence of Questionable Research Practices With Incentives for Truth Telling. Psychological Science, 23(5), 524-532. Sample sizes and Table 1 self-admission rates read from the author-hosted PDF at Carnegie Mellon.

Kataria, M. (2016). Confirmation: What's in the evidence? Journal of Behavioral and Experimental Economics, 65, 9-15. The published version was not obtained and is not open access. Every figure here is read from the identical working paper, Jena Economic Research Papers 2013-025, downloaded as a PDF.

Kerr, N. L. (1998). HARKing: Hypothesizing After the Results are Known. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 2(3), 196-217. Cited for the term and its definition, read as the abstract at Crossref; the full text was not obtained and no open copy was listed at Unpaywall.
Rubin, M. (2022). The Costs of HARKing. The British Journal for the Philosophy of Science, 73(2), 535-560. Read as the submitted version deposited at Zenodo.

Gelman, A., & Loken, E. (2014). The Statistical Crisis in Science. American Scientist, 102(6), 460. Quoted here for two sentences only; the working paper and the scanned article were both read, and the worked examples are set out at entry 560.

Thompson, W. C. (2009). Painting the target around the matching profile: the Texas sharpshooter fallacy in forensic DNA interpretation. Law, Probability and Risk, 8(3), 257-276. Only the abstract was obtained, read twice at the publisher; the PDF returned 403.

Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 4(2). Read as the full-text PDF in the Eindhoven University of Technology repository.
